#5140. US sanctions hit 41 companies accused of keeping Prince Group’s scam network running

Treasury says the network concealed ownership and sustained Prince Group operations, while US rules require covered assets to be blocked.

The US sanctioned four people and 41 entities on November 5, 2026, targeting a corporate network that Treasury says sustained Prince Group's operations after earlier sanctions. The designations subject covered assets to US blocking and reporting requirements, with restrictions also reaching companies that meet OFAC's ownership threshold.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said the network helped Prince Group, which it has designated a transnational criminal organization, manage offshore structures, conceal beneficial ownership and maintain commercial activities. It links the group's affiliates to digital asset investment scams, romance scams and other online fraud, with many operations relying on trafficked and coerced workers in Southeast Asian compounds.

The action follows earlier Prince Group sanctions on October 14, 2025 and June 23, 2026. The newly sanctioned individuals are Qiu Yong, Zhao Mengyao, He Yujing and Visal Pang, according to the OFAC designation record.

One chain runs from Qiu Yong through Sun Speed Holdings Limited, registered in the British Virgin Islands, to Hong Kong money lender Premium Financial Limited. Treasury says Qiu ultimately owns the lender and controls other BVI and Hong Kong companies on Prince Group's behalf.

Zhao serves as Qiu's personal assistant and as secretary and co-director of several Hong Kong companies he ultimately controls, Treasury said.

#5139. Why Bitcoin's Next Soft Fork Could Feel Like a Practice Run

Why Bitcoin's Next Soft Fork Could Feel Like a Practice Run

Four flaws in Bitcoin’s consensus rules that have lingered for years.

Issues like quantum resistance may command attention, but a practical cleanup is what many experts think Bitcoin’s next soft fork is likely to address, spanning fixes for vulnerabilities in the network’s difficulty adjustment mechanism to denial-of-service vectors among miners.

Proposed in 2019 and known as the Great Consensus Cleanup (BIP-54), the upgrade seeks to address the “cruft” in Bitcoin’s consensus design through changes that have historically been sidelined, as described by long-time Bitcoin developer and BIP-54 co-author Matt Corallo.

“There’s a laundry list of things we know of that we really need to clean up,” he said during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “All of these issues are real concerns that could impact Bitcoin negatively, but they’re not like, ‘Oh, the sky is falling.’”

Although a formal timeline for the BIP’s undertaking hasn’t been established, Corallo thinks there’s an 80% chance that the Great Consensus Cleanup is up next for the network. During his talk with Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke, he also called it a practical exercise for Bitcoin developers who haven’t yet been through a soft fork.

At its core, Corallo said BIP-54 “fixes some stuff that everyone agrees are problems,” while targeting four specific vulnerabilities:

Still, not everyone views a maintenance-focused soft fork as a major win. On X, Paul Sztorc, co-founder and CEO of LayerTwo Labs, called BIP-54’s potential activation “kind of depressing, since it is a janitorial maintenance fork that doesn't do anything.”

Surveying developers at TABconf in Atlanta, Sztorc noted that Bitcoin’s “best and brightest” predominantly expect the Great Consensus Cleanup to be Bitcoin’s next soft fork anyway, with the earliest estimate in September 2027, and most pointing to 2028 or later.

Following the activation of Taproot in 2021, Bitcoin’s community has faced years of gridlock surrounding protocol changes. This friction is frequently framed around “ossification,” with broader protocol changes like OP_CAT (BIP-347) and OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY (BIP-119) struggling to reach ecosystem-wide consensus.

According to Corallo, soft forks have always involved overcoming technical hurdles. But more recently, he’s observed political and social friction that’s become just as relevant.

The Bitcoin community spent months debating how Taproot should be activated, with arguments pitting miner-signaling thresholds against mandatory user flag days. Corallo argues that BIP-54 can establish a deployment playbook for future soft forks.

“In every recent soft fork, there’s also been a bunch of drama about activation mechanisms,” he said. “So hopefully we could do a soft fork to go through that drama, and then copy and paste and reuse it and head off some of that drama [for future soft forks].”

In that sense, BIP-54 is just as much about proving Bitcoin can still agree on upgrades at the social layer as it is about actual code cleanup.

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

Bitget users in Thailand face a December 5, 2026 access block, with the country's Securities and Exchange Commission urging customers to consider action on assets held on the exchange before the restriction takes effect.

Thailand's SEC set out the deadline in its November 5, 2026 notice after filing a criminal complaint over alleged unlicensed exchange operations. It said the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society had been notified to block bitget.com, other Bitget domains and the exchange's application. The scheduled restriction concerns access from Thailand. SEC announcement

The SEC identified BG Limited as Bitget's platform provider. It alleged that the exchange charged trading fees and targeted Thai users during 2022-2025 through a Thai-language website, baht-value displays and Thai-language promotions.

The complaint also names Kritsana Kritsananuwat, whom the SEC accused of helping promote the exchange through Facebook and YouTube. The allegations remain subject to the criminal process. The regulator described investigation by inquiry officials, prosecution by public prosecutors and adjudication by the courts as subsequent steps.

The SEC has asked customers to consider their holdings before access is blocked. Its notice specifies no asset freeze, compulsory sale or separate withdrawal cutoff, leaving customers to decide how to handle assets on the platform ahead of the scheduled restriction.

#5136. Argentine Bitcoiners Debut “The Genesis of Satoshi Nakamoto” Artwork in Downtown Buenos Aires

“The Genesis of Satoshi Nakamoto,” a 2.4-meter, multi-dimensional cube, was presented on October 29 at Polo Dot as part of the Open Fest of LABITCONF 2026. Driven by Bitcoin.ar through the Premio B·Arte, the work combines art, technology, and education in a journey through Bitcoin’s fundamental principles. The inauguration featured guided remarks by Rodolfo Andragnes and a musical performance by Mayumaná, according to an announcement by the organization.

Buenos Aires now has a monument dedicated to Satoshi Nakamoto, the person—or group of people—behind the creation of Bitcoin, whose identity remains unknown.

Driven by Bitcoin.ar through the fifth edition of the Premio B·Arte, the monument was conceived not only as a tribute to Satoshi, but also as an artistic and educational experience. Through its five faces—four lateral and one upper—it proposes a journey to approach different concepts that explain Bitcoin’s origin, functioning, and philosophy.

During the inauguration, Rodolfo Andragnes — co-founder of Bitcoin.ar and LABITCONF — accompanied the public with words and explanations about the details of the work, guiding the reading of its various elements and the meaning behind each representation. The presentation was accompanied by a musical show by Mayumaná, which added rhythm and sound to the opening of this new space dedicated to Bitcoin’s history.

Each of the monument’s faces offers a gateway to a different aspect of Bitcoin. The figure of Satoshi Nakamoto, for example, represents the anonymous character of its creator and the collective dimension of a technology that, once set in motion, continued to grow thanks to thousands of people distributed around the world. The reflections and multiplied geometric forms also evoke the structure of a network that replicates and expands.

Another of its faces addresses Bitcoin’s programmed scarcity through a cube that successively divides into halves in a Fibonacci sequence. The representation refers to “the halving”, the mechanism that approximately every four years halves the reward miners receive for validating blocks and that regulates the issuance of new bitcoins. Starting at 50 bitcoins per block, the total reward gets cut in half every four years for roughly 130 years, until 21 million bitcoins have been emitted and the block reward becomes zero. This supply limit is iconic to the cryptocurrency and key to its qualities as hard money.

The work also incorporates the first words of Bitcoin’s foundational document, the white paper published by Satoshi Nakamoto in October 31st,  2008. There, the possibility of making electronic payments directly between people, without needing to go through a financial institution, is proposed. That idea constitutes a foundational principle of the technology.

Another face reproduces information from the genesis block, the first block of the Bitcoin chain, created on January 3, 2009. Among its elements appears the reference to the headline from The Times newspaper that Satoshi incorporated into that block, a historical mark that places Bitcoin’s birth in its context and anchors it to history and time.

Thus, the monument proposes something more than contemplating a sculpture: it invites one to walk around it, observe it from different angles, and discover the concepts behind each of its parts; “The intention is to bring Bitcoin closer to those who are already part of its community, but also to awaken the curiosity of those who do not yet know its history.”

The monument was created by Ricardo Alonso, engineer, and Celeste Difabio Videla, architect, a couple of artists from Bariloche who won the fifth edition of the Premio B·Arte. The work measures 2.40 meters in width, length, and height, and is made of stainless steel and glass.

Its construction involved teams and collaborators from different localities across the country, in a process that combined different trades, materials, and techniques. Aída Pippo, visual artist, researcher of new technologies applied to art, and member of the Board of Directors of Bitcoin.ar, led the project and coordinated the different stages of production and assembly.

“It gives me great pride to feel that this is something we can leave in our city and in our country,” Andragnes expressed during the presentation, highlighting the value of a collective initiative that seeks to leave a cultural and educational footprint.

For their part, the creators noted that they sought for the work to function as a meeting point for the community and, at the same time, as a gateway for those who do not yet know Bitcoin. “You don’t always have the possibility of leaving something for posterity,” they shared when speaking of the experience of seeing the monument finished and installed in Buenos Aires.

With this inauguration, Bitcoin.ar seeks for the monument to become a permanent resource for the city: a space that schools, universities, families, and visitors can approach to learn Bitcoin’s history, discover its principles, and open new conversations about the future of money and technology. The intention is that what is presented today as an artistic work can continue to grow through educational activities and new experiences, and remain in Buenos Aires as a legacy for future generations.

The project was financed by the Fundación Bitcoin Iberoamérica and represents a new way of bringing Bitcoin’s history and principles to public and cultural spaces, beyond screens and specialized environments.

#5135. Erin and Sara Foster Reveal the Rule That Keeps Their Business—and Sisterhood—Working

The Nobody Wants This producers stop by the latest episode of The Huddle.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’ve binged all three seasons of the Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, presided over a board meeting in your chicest Favorite Daughter blazer, or nodded along to a cringey dating anecdote while listening to The World’s First Podcast, you are no doubt familiar with the work of multi-hyphenate sisters Erin and Sara Foster.

Raised in Los Angeles (dad is famous record producer David Foster), the sisters first gained notoriety with their VH1 mockumentary series, Barely Famous, in 2015. Since then, they’ve gone on to launch several successful businesses, including their clothing line and a production company, Fatigue Sisters Productions. (They even recently served as guest sharks on ABC’s Shark Tank.)

With the season 3 premiere of Nobody Wants This (based on Erin’s own experience of dating and marrying a Jewish man and later converting to Judaism), the dynamic duo stopped by the Women’s Health podcast The Huddle to chat with editors Abby Cuffey and Jacqueline Andriakos about doing business together, setting boundaries, and raising kids.

Erin and Sara launched their clothing line, Favorite Daughter, in late 2020 to fill gaps in their own closets. But as the company has grown and evolved over time, they’ve learned to put their customers at the heart of everything they do. It’s also forced the sisters to staff up with people who are willing to share their true opinions, rather than simply being yes-men or yes-women.

“That's something that is really challenging when you have a talent-focused brand,” Erin says. “It's taken a very long time for us to convince the people who work for us to be honest with us. That’s how people become monsters—no one's telling them the truth.”

“I always say, too, this is a democracy,” Sara adds. “This only works if everyone feels heard. This only works if you're allowed to do the thing that you're hired to do.”

Having a valued third or even fourth opinion also comes in handy when the two can’t see eye-to-eye, which happened often when the brand first launched.

“We’re in a good place today, but we would have blow-up screaming fights in fittings for many years at Favorite Daughter,” Erin says. “It’s tricky for us, because we do not have differentiated, carved-out roles. We have the exact same role, so if we disagree, it's really challenging to find the happy medium.”

In 2021, the sisters’ working relationship expanded further when they launched their podcast The World's First Podcast with Erin & Sara Foster. While the duo aren’t shy about diving into personal topics—be it romantic relationships or raising children—they have set certain boundaries to ensure their friends and family don’t end up embarrassed or as headline fodder.

“I have an idea of where [my husband’s] boundaries are,” Erin says. “He's not really into me talking about exes or other relationships.”

Sara, on the other hand, learned the hard way where one of her daughter’s boundaries lie when she revealed her juvenile arthritis diagnosis—in the hopes of helping other parents—and it was picked up by multiple outlets.

“It never occurred to me that that could happen,” Sara says. “My daughter was like, ‘I do not appreciate that.’ I was like, ‘Oh god, I'm so sorry.’”

Given that they have creative control over the podcast’s content, Erin and Sara do occasionally edit out portions that they think could be taken out of context with the TikTok-ification of media nowadays. “We try to err on the side of keeping things in, but then there's some times that you get a little ahead of yourself,” Erin says.

Speaking of raising daughters, Sara’s got even more wisdom to share on parenting—specifically about telling your kids the harsh truths about yourself.

“Being a mother is just such a exercise in getting humbled,” she says. “My instinct was always like, don't reveal yourself too much. Don't let them see your flaws. Don't tell them about all the times you f---ed up as a teenager yourself. But that's the opposite. You're really supposed to. Maybe some people disagree with this, but as they get older, you’re supposed to reveal mistakes you made, things that you wish you did differently... That has changed the dynamic with me and my older daughter—being honest with her about things that I wish I had done differently.”

Erin agrees: “I think it's probably better for your children to grow up knowing that you are a complicated, flawed person, and then you don't have to fall off a pedestal for them.”

To hear more from the sisters about how they find the creativity to create, their stance on kids and social media, and why they’re obsessed with a certain protein powder, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above!

#5134. Gold is still 25% below its peak even as demand reaches $188B in Q3

October's losses show why knowing who's buying gold is only part of understanding its price.

Central banks bought more gold in the third quarter of 2026 than consumers worldwide bought for jewelry.

According to the World Gold Council's latest demand report, central banks and other official institutions acquired an estimated net 321 metric tons, while jewelry consumption came to 313 tons.

In the same quarter a year earlier, jewelry buyers had consumed about 150 tons more than central banks acquired.

By September, the institutions buying gold for their reserves had overtaken the people buying it to wear, although roughly 63% of estimated official demand couldn't be traced through publicly reported country-level purchases.

The price barely kept pace with Bitcoin, which gained 42.7% during the quarter versus gold's 3.84%. Both attracted money through exchange-traded funds, so this wasn't a straightforward case of investors ditching one for the other. They bought both and got different results.

However, Bitcoin's lead came crashing down in October: gold fell 6.3%, while Bitcoin lost 7.3%. Governments kept accumulating bullion, and investors kept believing in scarce assets, but neither belief did much for that month's returns.

The buyers behind those beliefs, and their reasons for holding on, explain rather more than the safe-haven label does.

Global gold demand reached $188 billion in the third quarter, up 22% from a year earlier. That sounds like an impressive shopping spree until you weigh the purchases.

Buyers took home 1% less metal, at 1,369 tons, while the average quarterly price was 23% higher. Much of the extra spending covered the price increase rather than buying more gold.

That was especially apparent in jewelry, where consumption fell 17% to 313 tons, the weakest third quarter in the council's records since 2000. Buyers in China and India cut purchases or chose lighter and lower-carat pieces, adjusting what they bought to what they could afford.

Physical investment wasn't immune either: demand for bars and coins fell 19% to 268 tons. Paying more per ounce didn't make every buyer more eager to own one.

Central banks' net purchases rose 42% to 321 tons, while gold-backed ETFs added 211 tons, reversing the previous quarter's withdrawals.

Those purchases helped offset weaker demand from jewelry buyers and physical investors, giving the market support from buyers who wanted gold as a financial holding even as others balked at the cost.

The categories don't divide neatly into institutions buying and households retreating. Individuals own gold through ETFs, and institutions can own bars and coins.

But the numbers do show that demand weakened in traditional consumer and physical-investment markets, while official reserves and listed funds absorbed more metal. Gold was becoming a harder purchase to justify at the counter and an easier allocation to defend in a portfolio.

Of the estimated 321 tons in net purchases, only about 120 tons appeared in publicly reported country-level activity.

China disclosed additions of 63 tons and Poland 40 tons, making them the largest reported buyers, but the country disclosures leave approximately 201 tons of the council's estimate unaccounted for in the public figures.

Reporting delays and purchases governments don't disclose can explain activity missing from the country data, and the broader estimate may be revised. The gap alone also doesn't establish secret, coordinated purchases.

We have a much better estimate of the total than a complete account of who bought it, which limits how confidently we can interpret the buying.

Q3 2026 net official demand, using rounded inputs: 321 metric tons estimated in total, of which 120 were publicly reported. The remaining 201 are calculated by subtraction, not added to the total. Unreported activity can include delayed or undisclosed purchases; estimates may be revised.

Source: World Gold Council, Q3 2026 central-bank demand

Central banks acquired an estimated 675 tons in the first nine months of 2026, exceeding their purchases over the same period of 2025.

Their appetite is large enough to offset weakness elsewhere, but incomplete disclosures make it harder to attribute that appetite to particular governments or motives. The survey evidence offers more detail on the latter, with some important limits of its own.

Quarterly totals. Jewelry measures consumption; bars and coins, ETFs, and official institutions measure net demand. Negative ETF values mean net withdrawals. Official institutions include central banks. These selected channels do not exhaust total gold demand and do not separate household from institutional investors.

Source: World Gold Council / Metals Focus / Refinitiv GFMS, Q3 2026, Table 1

In the World Gold Council's 2026 central-bank survey, 74% of respondents expected the US dollar's share of global reserves to be lower in five years. That gives some basis for the argument that reserve managers want less dependence on the dollar.

The IMF's second-quarter foreign-exchange reserve data put the dollar's share at 56.7%, down from 57.18% in the preceding quarter. It remained the dominant reserve currency, with dollar holdings largely steady as holdings in other currencies expanded.

This series also excludes monetary gold, so it can't tell us how much gold replaced dollars.

Even the funding of gold purchases is less straightforward than the familiar sell-Treasuries-buy-bullion argument allows. Half the survey respondents said they'd finance new gold purchases through domestic programs using local currency, while 38% said they'd sell existing reserve assets.

Buying locally produced gold with local currency doesn't require a corresponding sale of US government debt, and the quarterly demand totals can't identify what financed every purchase.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Reserve managers can want more gold without wanting out of everything else. Bullion gives them an asset whose value doesn't depend on an issuer honoring a financial obligation, making it a way to reduce reliance on other governments' currencies and debt.

However, the bargain still includes a market price, and that price can fall enough to make the word “protection” feel rather generous over shorter periods.

Gold finished October at $3,913 an ounce, down 6.3% for the month and roughly 25% below its January peak, according to the World Gold Council's November market commentary.

Central bank demand hadn't spared holders that loss, because even a persistent buyer can't dictate the price everyone else trades at. Futures positions and the need to raise cash can overwhelm the reassurance of a government adding bullion to its reserves.

Global gold-backed ETFs attracted $2.7 billion in net inflows during October, adding 19 tons and taking holdings to a record 4,275 tons. Their combined assets under management still fell 6% to $542 billion, as the lower gold price more than offset the new money.

The funds held more metal and were worth less, an entirely possible outcome that gets lost when inflows are treated as a verdict on returns.

The broader point is consistent with a July 2026 IMF study, which found that gold's ability to hedge market risk depends on the shock and the economic conditions around it. Gold can help diversify a reserve portfolio over time without reliably sheltering it during extreme stress.

Someone reducing exposure to sovereign credit over several years and someone trying to avoid a loss this month may buy the same asset, but they're asking it to do different jobs.

Bitcoin gave investors a much better third quarter, gaining 42.7% to end September around $83,570, according to 21Shares' quarterly analysis.

US spot Bitcoin ETFs added about 79,800 BTC, worth about $6.2 billion, reversing roughly $4.8 billion in second-quarter withdrawals.

Their purchases were nearly twice the estimated 41,300 BTC newly mined over the period, giving the rally a measurable source of demand through funds available to professional and individual investors alike.

That comparison with new supply is striking, although newly mined coins are only one source of Bitcoin available to buy. Existing holders own a far larger stock, and some were reducing their positions while ETFs accumulated.

21Shares estimated that balances in the long-term-holder cohort fell by 248,000 BTC during the quarter. The figure isn't a direct count of exchange sales, since coins can leave the cohort through transfers or other classification effects, but it prevents ETF buying from being mistaken for a market in which everyone was adding to their holdings.

Global gold-backed funds attracted a record $31 billion in third-quarter inflows and added 211 tons of bullion, even as the metal's price gain fell well short of Bitcoin's.

The dollar totals cover different markets: the gold figure is global, while the Bitcoin figure covers US spot ETFs. Their respective market sizes and investor bases differ too, so treating the totals as a head-to-head contest would tell us little.

Investors added exposure to both assets, but their quarterly returns differed by nearly 39%, which offers little support for a simple account of Bitcoin rallying because money was leaving gold. It also limits what ETF data alone can explain.

Listed funds supplied demand in both markets, while trading elsewhere, including derivatives positions and borrowed money, helped determine how far each price moved.

October narrowed that enormous performance gap in an unwelcome way. Bitcoin fell 7.3% to about $77,500, while gold lost 6.3% over the same month.

Reported October 2026 returns in US dollars. Gold uses the LBMA PM benchmark through Oct. 30, the last business day; Bitcoin trades continuously. These are price returns, excluding fees and income, rather than ETF returns. Similar losses in one month do not establish a lasting correlation or a common cause.

Source: World Gold Council / Bloomberg / LBMA, October 2026, Table 1 · 21Shares, November 2026 Bitcoin outlook

Gold ETFs continued to attract net investment globally, led by Europe and Asia, while North American funds recorded modest withdrawals. On Nov. 4, Reuters reported that the largest Bitcoin-backed funds tracked by LSEG/Lipper lost $215 million in October.

While the totals don't establish that investors moved money from Bitcoin to gold, they show that net buying persisted across global bullion funds while the tracked Bitcoin funds lost money to withdrawals.

The World Gold Council pointed to reductions in speculative positions, revised expectations for Federal Reserve policy, and rotation between assets as possible contributors to gold's decline.

Bitcoin contended with weaker tech stocks, tighter credit conditions, the Binance hack, and the US midterm elections. Different sellers had different reasons to act, even though holders of both assets ended the month with losses.

Scarcity offers little defense against someone who needs cash or wants less exposure to volatile markets. Central-bank purchases can absorb gold without guaranteeing its price, just as Bitcoin's supply limit can constrain issuance without guaranteeing buyers at the price its holders would prefer.

October put both propositions on display, even while some investors continued to add bullion to their portfolios.

The sovereign comparison needs a careful approach, because a government owning Bitcoin doesn't necessarily mean it has entered the market to buy it.

The US established a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve in March 2025, formally giving Bitcoin a place among assets the federal government can retain and manage.

However, the executive order creating the reserve directed that it be funded primarily with Bitcoin already held through criminal or civil asset forfeitures.

Officials were also authorized to devise budget-neutral ways to acquire additional Bitcoin without incremental taxpayer costs. That permission and the decision to retain existing coins have policy importance, but neither establishes a recurring purchase program comparable with central banks adding gold to their reserves.

That's why putting seized Bitcoin into a reserve can happen without buying a single additional coin on the market.

The World Gold Council's quarterly figures estimate net additions to official gold holdings. The US reserve order governs, in large part, what happens to assets the government already owns.

Gold already has an established role in central bank balance sheets and reserve management. Bitcoin's newer sovereign role could evolve, but ETF access, government recognition, and official purchases each affect demand through a different route.

Investors can't assume progress on one will produce the buying associated with another, however attractive the reserve announcement sounds.

Interest-rate expectations and access to cash will continue to test both markets. Stronger US employment or inflation readings can encourage expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy, increasing the appeal of interest-bearing assets relative to gold and potentially making financial conditions less accommodating for Bitcoin.

Weaker readings can support expectations of easier policy, although a deterioration severe enough to prompt fears of an economic slowdown can also leave investors wanting cash.

Neither the gold-demand report nor Bitcoin's ETF inflows can settle how investors will react to the next release. They can tell us more about who has been buying and how readily those buyers might leave.

Central banks can accumulate gold over several years, while ETF investors can cut exposure much faster. Consumers can buy lighter jewelry, and traders using borrowed money can face demands to reduce positions precisely when they'd prefer to wait.

That mix helps explain why persistent belief in an asset can coexist with a sharp fall in its price.

The reserve manager diversifying away from another government's obligations may have little reason to sell bullion during a correction, while an investor facing losses elsewhere may sell the same metal because it's readily tradable.

Bitcoin's fixed supply doesn't remove that need for cash, and official recognition doesn't give its holders the resources or mandate to ride out every downturn.

Central banks overtaking jewelry buyers shows how gold demand is being redistributed, and October's losses show the limits of what those purchases can promise other holders.

Someone buying for protection needs the asset's behavior to fit the risk they're trying to reduce and the period they can afford to hold it.

Gold can serve a reserve manager well over years and disappoint an investor over weeks, while Bitcoin can deliver a spectacular quarter without becoming a dependable place to wait out the next sell-off.

#5133. Arkansas Sues Kalshi, Joining a Growing List of States Targeting Prediction Markets

Arkansas Sues Kalshi, Joining a Growing List of States Targeting Prediction Markets

Arkansas has sued Kalshi, accusing the prediction market of offering an illegal, unregulated gambling platform to the state's residents, Attorney General Tim Griffin said on Wednesday.

The lawsuit, filed against KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc., alleges multiple violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. The state is seeking restitution, penalties, taxes and an injunction.

Today I filed a lawsuit against @Kalshi for violating the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act by operating an unregulated gambling platform.

Kalshi has built a global business that it calls a prediction market, allowing consumers to wager money on the outcome of just about… pic.twitter.com/ePycNKXzy6

— Attorney General Tim Griffin (@AGTimGriffin) November 4, 2026

"It doesn't take a genius to understand that wagering money on whether the Razorbacks win or lose is gambling," Griffin said. "And gambling on an unregulated platform is squarely prohibited by Arkansas law."

Instead of obtaining licenses and paying the taxes required of gambling operators, Kalshi opened its platform to Arkansas residents as young as 18 and encouraged them to bet on sporting and entertainment events, Griffin alleged. "Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics," he said.

Griffin pointed to Kalshi's own responsible-gambling tools, including self-exclusion, deposit limits and trading breaks, along with its partnership with the National Council on Problem Gambling, as evidence that the company knows its platform carries gambling-style risks. "Although Kalshi insists that its products are not gambling, its actions speak louder than its labels," he said.

Kalshi, which is regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, has argued in other cases that its event contracts fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction and are not subject to state gambling laws.

Arkansas is the latest of more than a dozen states to take on prediction markets. Among the most significant cases:

Other states have also moved against prediction markets. Arizona filed criminal charges against Kalshi in March, a Washington court temporarily blocked its sports contracts in July, and Massachusetts' case is now before the state's highest court after a lower court barred Kalshi's sports contracts in January.

The CFTC has sued at least 10 states to defend what it says is its exclusive authority over prediction markets, and President Donald Trump has backed the agency, calling several state officials who challenged the platforms "scum."

Federal appeals courts are split. The Third Circuit ruled in April that New Jersey cannot regulate Kalshi's sports contracts, while the Sixth and Ninth Circuits sided with Ohio, Tennessee and Nevada. New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to settle the question, backed by 39 other states and the District of Columbia, as well as the NFL. Kalshi's response to the petition is due November 9, and the Supreme Court is not expected to decide whether to take up the case until December at the earliest, ESPN reported.

#5132. A single AI forecast inflates US power auctions by $5.7B

AI demand is pushing up computer costs and straining electricity markets, and the spending boom is creating new inflation pressures.

Australia's latest inflation figures showed that prices in the category covering audio, visual, and computing equipment rose 6.1% in a single quarter.

That's by far the largest increase in the Australian Bureau of Statistics series, which began in 1980. Computers, TVs, and electronics in general have gotten cheaper and delivered more performance for the same money.

Customers around the world, including Australia, have (reasonably) expected this trend to continue.

This is why the third quarter came as such a surprise, as it interrupted a consumer expectation that has been in place for decades.

The Reserve Bank of Australia linked higher prices for some computers and other consumer electronics to rising memory-chip costs associated with demand for AI infrastructure.

The same components, or the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them, are now being pursued by companies whose shopping budgets look nothing like yours.

On Nov. 3, the RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85%, citing AI-related investment as one of several sources of price pressure. Higher fuel costs and domestic capacity constraints were also involved, and the bank said AI's effect on overall consumer prices remained modest.

The technology hasn't single-handedly taken over Australian monetary policy, although it has progressed from a promise in investor presentations to a consideration in decisions that affect ordinary borrowers.

We've also seen this in the US, where AI demand has reached much further into the system that determines the cost of electricity. PJM, the grid operator serving all or parts of 13 states and Washington, D.C., runs auctions that pay power plants and other resources to be available when the grid needs them, years before the electricity is actually used.

In its analysis of this summer's auction, PJM’s independent market monitor calculated that power providers would receive about $16.4 billion for making capacity available during the 2028-29 delivery year.

The monitor then reran the auction without the forecast growth in demand from new and expanding data centers, while leaving existing data-center demand in place.

Under that scenario, the total fell to roughly $10.7 billion, down $5.7 billion. The calculation shows how expectations of future data-center demand can affect the price of keeping power available.

Together, the Australian prices and the American auction show how big AI's effect on inflation is: the spending starts producing identifiable, quantifiable consequences long before we see any productivity gains.

The costs also reach people who aren't buying AI services, while the institutions assigning those costs are still working out how much responsibility the companies requesting the infrastructure should carry.

Data centers are buildings packed with computing equipment, along with the cooling systems and electricity connections needed to keep it working.

However, AI demand extends well beyond the GPUs that attract most of the attention.

Filling a data center with expensive chips also requires the hardware that feeds them information and keeps them running, creating competition for parts and factory capacity that other electronics manufacturers depend on.

The RBA's account follows that competition through to Australian shops, where higher memory costs contributed to more expensive consumer electronics.

The ABS's 6.1% quarterly equipment-price increase covers a particular statistical category, so it can't be treated as the price increase for every computer, much less a precise measurement of AI's contribution. It does, however, give the central bank's explanation an observable consumer outcome.

Again, something similar has been happening in the US. The September consumer-price report recorded a 9.7% annual increase for computers, peripherals, and smart-home assistants, while smartphone prices were 9.9% lower than a year earlier.

CPI-U price changes from September 2025 to September 2026, not seasonally adjusted. The all-items index provides a benchmark for the two product categories. These movements do not isolate AI's contribution to prices.

Source: BLS, September 2026 CPI release, Table 2

But even though we've seen large increases in the affected categories, they've actually had a relatively small effect on the average household's entire spending basket.

The San Francisco Fed calculated that prices for information-processing equipment rose 13% over the year to August, but added only 0.2 percentage points to that month's 3.4% headline inflation rate under the personal consumption expenditures measure. Its economists found limited evidence that those pressures had spread broadly across the economy, where energy costs and tariff-related goods prices were doing considerably more of the damage.

The Bank of England was also monitoring demand for AI components as a source of global cost pressure, but judged the potential effect of these and other non-energy risks on UK inflation to be much smaller than the energy shock and little changed since September.

Its quarter-point increase in Bank Rate to 4% was justified by energy-driven inflation risks, alongside stronger-than-expected activity.

Another complication in software is that a subscription can become more expensive when it starts doing something its previous version couldn't.

Federal Reserve researchers have warned that parts of the inflation data may not adequately account for those improvements. Paying more can still hurt a household budget, even when part of the increase reflects better quality.

Electricity is another way costs can spread because both new and existing customers depend on the same system. Someone replacing a laptop can postpone the purchase, whereas households connected to a grid that accommodates substantial new demand have far less control over what gets built and how the resulting costs reach them.

PJM coordinates the power system across much of the eastern US, and one of its jobs is to make sure enough electricity can be supplied when demand is high.

Alongside markets for delivered electricity, it runs auctions that pay suppliers to commit capacity for a future year, meaning they agree to be available under the market's rules when the system needs them.

That availability has a separate price from the electricity eventually generated. Power stations need sufficient revenue to remain in service or justify investment, while the operator has to plan before households and businesses switch on equipment that will require supply.

Forecasting how much power customers will need therefore becomes part of a financial transaction.

PJM's July auction for the 2028-29 delivery year produced approximately $16.41 billion in auction revenue. In a recent analysis, its independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, reran the auction without the forecast growth in demand from new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, while leaving other assumptions unchanged.

The resulting revenue fell to approximately $10.7 billion, a modeled difference of $5.7 billion for that delivery year.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Revenue for the 2028–29 capacity delivery year. The counterfactual removes forecast growth from new and expanding data centers, retains existing load, and holds other assumptions fixed. The gap is a modeled capacity-market effect, not a household surcharge or an estimate of AI alone.

Source: Monitoring Analytics, October 30, 2026, Table 11, scenarios 0 and 3

The calculation shows how the forecast growth affects revenue inside the monitor's model, using the auction's rules and its existing assumptions about available supply.

While these numbers are only an estimate of generative AI demand, the financial exposure is still substantial, and it starts with demand expectations rather than requiring every proposed building to be operating.

Planning too little capacity creates an obvious risk of shortages, while planning for projects that consume much less power than expected can leave expensive infrastructure with fewer customers than its financing assumed.

Those decisions reach households through utilities and electricity suppliers, with the eventual effect depending on contracts and local regulation.

Capacity payments are one part of power costs, so an increase in that market can't simply be relabeled as the same percentage increase in a residential bill. Customers whose suppliers have already secured power under contracts may see a different result from customers more directly exposed to new market prices.

Virginia regulators have established a separate rate class for Dominion Energy Virginia's large users and requirements intended to make them cover more of the costs associated with serving them, including minimum payments and contractual safeguards.

The requirement to take and pay for electricity for at least 14 years applies to new large-load customers contracting for service on or after Jan. 1, 2027.

Those eligibility rules determine which projects the safeguards cover and whether other customers remain exposed if a developer reserves substantial capacity and subsequently needs less of it.

Tech companies can pay their own invoices and still affect prices elsewhere, because increased demand can require more expensive supply or new shared infrastructure.

Equally, a large customer making reliable long-term payments can help spread existing costs across more consumption, which is why the evidence doesn't support treating every data center as an automatic surcharge on the neighborhood.

The MIT working paper revised in October estimated that data-center entry raised residential electricity rates by 2.1%, with larger effects among investor-owned utilities, using data from 2010 through 2024.

Researchers behind another working paper, using a different method and covering 2015 through 2024, estimated a modest average reduction in retail rates and warned that future supply constraints could reverse that effect.

However, both studies analyzed different units and used different methods to identify the effect. Also, both studies largely precede the current scale of AI expansion and data center construction.

Their disagreement on the data is a good reason to look at local systems and the rules governing them, rather than choosing whichever national average makes the most satisfying claim.

Someone using AI to complete a task faster has experienced a real benefit, but turning that saved time into lower prices across an economy will take a lot more time.

Businesses have to organize work around the technology, produce more with the resources they have, and pass some of the resulting savings to customers rather than retaining all of them.

We are yet to see that transition happen. A survey of nearly 6,000 executives across four countries found that 89% reported no effect on their firm's productivity over the previous three years, while other Fed-linked research found evidence consistent with productivity gains among adopters.

In its Nov. 5 preliminary release, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm business labor productivity rose 3.6% in the third quarter, while unit labor costs fell 0.7%, both at seasonally adjusted annualized rates. Businesses produced more per hour worked, with labor compensation per unit of output declining.

However, the release doesn't identify how much AI contributed to those gains or establish how much of the savings reached customers.

Nonfarm business sector, percent change from the previous quarter at a seasonally adjusted annual rate. Figures use the November 5, 2026 release; Q3 2026 is preliminary. The series measure output per hour and compensation per unit of output, without identifying AI's contribution or savings passed to consumers.

Source: BLS, Productivity and Costs, November 5, 2026, Table 2

Even widespread productivity improvements wouldn't automatically produce an equally large fall in inflation.

Fed Governor Lisa Cook explained in September that expectations of higher future incomes and returns can encourage more spending today, adding demand alongside the technology's eventual increase in supply.

Companies are already investing in anticipation of those gains, while households holding appreciated assets may also be more willing to spend.

The RBA expects data-center investment to support business activity, but estimates that roughly 70% of the additional investment will be imported, limiting the direct boost to domestic production even as local construction requires labor and materials.

Its November decision addressed a broader inflation problem, with AI contributing to particular pressures in an economy already facing plenty of others.

The companies building AI are making private bets on future demand, while regulators and utilities must decide how much of the infrastructure required to meet those bets other customers should pay for.

While greater productivity could eventually benefit households and businesses far beyond the technology industry, those future gains don't settle who should pay for grid expansion, or who pays if a project requests more power than it needs.

#5131. I’m Running the New York City Marathon Topless. The Reason Is Not What You Think.

It was my 18-mile long run, the farthest I'd gone so far in my New York City Marathon training, when I felt anxiety creep into my ankles. Central Park was full of life and happiness, but I was suddenly acutely aware of every mile, every ache, and every vulnerability I couldn't outrun. “I could just stop right now,” I thought.

A year earlier, I was in active treatment for breast cancer at 32. I had undergone chemotherapy, a mastectomy, and reconstruction, and was still learning to recognize my new body. Now, I was preparing to run 26.2 miles, completely topless, with my scars visible.

But I pushed through the fear: This was exactly why I chose to run in the first place. Not because I’ve overcome everything or that I have nothing left to hide—but because I’m learning to show up as I am: Uncomfortable, imperfect, and still moving forward. I’m running like this in the hopes that my story might help save another woman’s life. If seeing me and learning about my journey helps her speak up or look into her own breast cancer risk, this run becomes bigger than me.

In 2023, I left my career as an associate in wealth management at Merrill Lynch to raise my son. Six short months after I resigned, everything changed.

I found a lump. My ob-gyn told me I was too young for a mammogram. An ultrasound came back benign. It was a third doctor, a breast surgeon, who finally took me seriously and sent me for a mammogram, a biopsy, and an MRI. She saved my life.

I was leaving the gym on an ordinary Thursday when the call came. I had breast cancer in both breasts: stage 2 triple-negative cancer on one side and stage 1 ER/PR-positive cancer on the other.

The world went blurry, and every sound was muffled. Was I dying? My son was only one. I couldn't leave him without a mother, and my husband without his partner. I had so much more life to live, and so much more to do. How had the first two appointments missed this?

My husband, Elio, and I built my care team at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and together we mapped out a plan: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and surgeries. Each decision I made along the way helped me feel a little more in control.

One of the hardest parts of treatment was confronting how much my body had changed. When I finally had my mastectomy, I braced myself to be horrified when the bandages came off. I shed one tear. It hit me that things would never be the same and that a part of my body I'd tied to my femininity and sexuality had been changed forever. I faced a choice no woman should have to make. For me, it was this or facing my mortality.

But the moment that still gets me isn't the one in front of the mirror. It was the afternoon my then-two-year-old son caught a glimpse of my chest.

"Mommy, you have a boo boo?” He asked. “Are you hurt? Do you need to go to the hosminal?"

I had tried to protect my son from knowing what I was going through—no two-year-old should have to learn what cancer is before they learn the alphabet. But still, he could tell something was wrong. I was proud of his sympathy and awareness, but at the same time, I was heartbroken he noticed. I dreaded telling him about my cancer diagnosis—especially given my BRCA diagnosis and the unknowns about whether I had passed it along to him.

Later, changing in a gym locker room for the first time since surgery, I flinched, covering my chest as I pulled off my sports bra. I never would have done that before cancer. Was I ashamed of the scars? Nervous that I looked different? Probably a bit of both. I gave myself grace for that instinctive reaction, but also promised myself then that I would no longer let shame drive how I felt about my body. My scars are evidence that I lived. They stand for tenacity, resilience, and bravery—traits I want my son to have and how I want him to remember me.

During treatment, I set a goal to run my first half marathon a few months after my mastectomy. It kept me focused and gave me something to look forward to, something beyond appointments, medications, and the uncertainty of treatment. Crossing the finish line felt powerful. I thought of all the work that I’d put in to get there and the many training sessions where I chose to show up for myself every day.

But shortly after, I was disappointed to learn I would need to continue oral chemotherapy to help reduce the risk of recurrence. This pushed my recovery timeline back and meant I’d have to wait longer for my reconstructive surgeries. So I set another goal: if I could run 13.1 miles, I could run 26.2 the following year, when I’d be done with treatment and surgeries.

I decided I would also run topless, putting on display the very thing I vowed to never hide. No shirt, no bra. To prevent chafing and provide makeshift support, I plan on using special styling tape donated by NOOD.

I would do it for the women who might have questions they want to ask their doctors, who feel like something isn’t right but keep minimizing their concerns. And I would also do it for the other survivors out there. I hope that by seeing me run, they also feel more comfortable in their bodies, scars and all.

I set my sights on the New York City Marathon, running with Fred’s Team, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center’s charity partner. I even created a subteam, Team Laklak, named after the beauty brand I co-founded during my cancer journey, offering science-based makeup that’s still full of color and fun. I’m proud that we’ve raised $45,000 to date for the very hospital that saved my life. It feels like such a full-circle moment that the beauty company I dreamed up while sitting in treatment chairs there can now give back to other women in this way.

I’m not the first woman to run a marathon topless, but I will be the first in New York City. In 2024, Louise Butcher also ran the London Marathon, showing off the scars from her mastectomy and flat closure reconstruction for similar reasons. I chose to reconstruct with implants—and I’m not sure if people will find my run more taboo or sexualized because of it. They shouldn’t. Louise and I faced the same disease and underwent similar treatments.

On November 1, I'll finish my 26.2 miles back in Central Park, the same park where I once thought, “I could just stop right now.”

My story is about more than learning to embrace my body after cancer. It's also about what can happen when women are dismissed, when they question their instincts, or when they assume they are too young to be at risk.

Breast cancer doesn't discriminate by age. Approximately one in eight women in the United States will be diagnosed in their lifetime, and a diagnosis can happen well before the age many women associate with routine screening. I was fortunate to find a breast surgeon who listened to me and pursued further testing, but not every woman knows what questions to ask or where to turn when something doesn't feel right. A breast cancer risk assessment tool can be a useful place to start. While it cannot diagnose cancer or replace medical advice from a physician, it can help women better understand their personal risk and discuss whether additional evaluation or screening may be appropriate.

Whether we're navigating cancer or chasing a marathon finish line, we will all have moments when we want to stop. We may not feel fearless or ready. We may not know exactly what comes next. But we can take the next step, ask the next question, and learn to trust ourselves along the way.

I'm running topless because I no longer want to hide my scars. I'm running because I'm still here and because I can. But most of all, I'm doing this in the hope that another woman will feel a little more empowered to take charge of her own story.

Lauren Spiezia is a breast cancer survivor who carries the BRCA2 mutation and the founder of Laklak Beauty, a clean cosmetic brand built from her experience as an oncology patient. More at laklakbeauty.com/run.

#5130. South Korean Crypto Exchange Gopax Suspends Withdrawals and Trading After Hacking Threat

South Korea's Gopax halted standard withdrawals at 2:55 p.m. and trading at 3:53 p.m. Friday after a hacking-threat email, and is transferring all held assets to cold wallets with no loss reported so far.

South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Gopax suspended withdrawals and trading on Friday after receiving a hacking-threat email, and said it is moving all held virtual assets into offline cold wallets as a preemptive step to protect customer funds.

Gopax halted standard deposit and withdrawal services at 2:55 p.m. local time and stopped trading at 3:53 p.m., Yonhap News Agency reported, citing the exchange. Direct withdrawals through the website and app are unavailable. Customers who want coins out must apply through the customer support center, where requests are processed manually after internal verification.

“To ensure the safe custody of user assets, we plan to transfer all virtual assets to cold wallets for storage,” Gopax said in remarks carried by Seoul Economic Daily. “Direct withdrawals through the Gopax website or app are temporarily unavailable, and customers wishing to withdraw funds should apply through the Gopax customer support center.”

No actual loss of assets has been reported. The company has not set a date to reopen trading or standard withdrawals.

With trading offline, all open orders were canceled, Chosun Biz reported. Deposits were initially paused with withdrawals; later Korean coverage said deposits had been restored while web and app withdrawals stayed shut. Manual withdrawals through support will take longer than usual.

A cold wallet is a storage setup kept offline, cut off from the internet that hot wallets use to process customer sends. Gopax said the shift of remaining hot-wallet balances into cold storage is meant to shrink the surface available to anyone who can reach online systems.

A Gopax official told Yonhap the email came from a party claiming it could hack the exchange, but that the threat itself had not been verified. “We ask for your understanding, as this measure is intended to prevent financial incidents and protect user assets,” the company said.

The freeze lands in a week when exchange security is already under a bright light. On Oct. 29, attackers drained about $6.34 billion from Binance hot wallets in what Binance later described as a months-long campaign that began with a fake job interview. The FBI has tied that theft to North Korea; Binance has reopened withdrawals in stages and said it is covering customer losses from its own funds.

Brazil’s Mercado Bitcoin froze deposits and withdrawals earlier this week after its own security incident, with preliminary estimates of suspicious transfers near $40 million. Gopax’s case is different on the facts disclosed so far: the exchange is describing a threat email and a precautionary lockdown, not a confirmed drain.

Gopax itself has been dealing with account trouble. From early September, abnormal access hit some user accounts, leaking personal information on seven customers and two current or former employees, with further leakage confirmed last month, Yonhap’s Korean dispatch said. The company has treated that breach as separate from Friday’s threat email; any link has not been confirmed.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has also been pressing domestic platforms after a broader wave of cybersecurity incidents across financial firms. Korean exchanges are already required to keep at least 80% of customer crypto in cold storage. Friday’s move pushes Gopax further offline while it checks whether the threat is real.

For bitcoin holders on Gopax, the practical effect is a queue: coins are being parked offline while support staff approve outbound sends one by one. That is slower than an app button, and it is the trade the exchange says it is making to keep balances intact.

The test for Gopax now is whether it can finish the cold-wallet transfer, clear the manual withdrawal queue without a loss, and say when trading comes back — or whether the unverified threat turns into the incident it was trying to get ahead of.

#5129. Nvidia’s CEO, an alleged romance and a suspected Chinese spy: Congress wants answers

The reported intelligence memo adds detail to an earlier House briefing request, with an answer sought by November 11.

Congress is seeking answers about Nvidia’s defenses against espionage as Financial Times reporting describes an intelligence-based memo alleging a romantic relationship between CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed.

FT excerpts shared by @AsiaLens on November 7 report that US intelligence believes Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, citing people familiar with the matter.

Three House committee chairs signed a November 4 letter requesting a joint, closed-door briefing on Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage. Published on November 5, the request predates the FT excerpts.

Nvidia has described the contacts as ordinary customer business and said it does not share classified information. The central security question is whether the alleged relationship provided access beyond ordinary customer contact.

The FT excerpts shared by @AsiaLens say US officials wrote the memo earlier in 2026 using information obtained by American intelligence. People familiar with the memo said it alleged Huang had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer.

According to the same excerpts, the memo reached a small group of senior US officials shortly before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping. The memo itself is not public, and its exact date and authoring agency are not established. The reported assessment and relationship allegation have not been publicly proven.

The letter was signed by Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence committees, respectively. Their public release identifies possible foreign-adversary access to US technology and information as the reason for seeking the briefing.

A November 4 letter preceded the FT excerpts shared on November 7. Explore the lawmakers’ request and Nvidia’s stated limits on customer access.

The November 4 letter asks about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage.

In its November 5 statement to CNBC, Nvidia described ordinary customer information and denied sharing sensitive trade secrets or national-security information.

The next requested step is an answer by November 11. A November 18 briefing remains proposed, with attendance unconfirmed.

#5128. Canadian Man Extradited to US Over Plot to Hijack University Supercomputers for Crypto

Canadian Man Extradited to US Over Plot to Hijack University Supercomputers for Crypto

A Canadian man has been extradited to the United States to face charges that he helped hack into university computers to steal login credentials and secretly mine cryptocurrency, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.

A federal grand jury in the Western District of New York indicted Ryan James Roach, 35, of Saskatchewan, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario, on charges of conspiracy to obtain information from and damage a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentionally damaging a protected computer. The charges carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

Canadian man extradited to the U.S. for his role in computer hacking scheme targeting universities... @FBIBuffalo @USDOJ_Intl https://t.co/vY8IacXdZZ pic.twitter.com/NsSZ5BIkIf

Between June 2016 and December 2019, the pair targeted U.S. educational institutions with supercomputers, researching security weaknesses in their networks before breaking in, according to the indictment. Once inside, they allegedly deployed malware, stole login credentials and forced the victims' computers to mine cryptocurrency for their own benefit.

Victims included institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts, among them a university in the Western District of New York, prosecutors said. The pair allegedly used virtual private servers in several countries, registered under false names, to send malware and mining software to victim computers and store stolen credentials, and routed attacks through computers compromised at other victims to hide their identities.

Roach was extradited from Canada on October 28 and arraigned in Rochester, New York, where he was held pending a detention hearing. Extradition proceedings against Stubbings are continuing in Canada.

The scheme is a form of cryptojacking, in which attackers use other people's computers to mine crypto while the victims bear the electricity costs and slower performance. The Justice Department did not say which cryptocurrency the pair allegedly mined.

But hackers looking to profit from stolen computing power may be turning elsewhere. In a report published Monday, Google's Threat Intelligence Group said it expects attackers to "increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking," hijacking companies' access to AI models and passing on the bills.

Unlike the gradual drain of cryptojacking, LLMjacking can run up huge cloud charges within hours, Google said. In incidents investigated by its Mandiant unit this year, fraudulent charges topped $100,000 in a single day, and some organizations racked up $1 million before access was cut off. Attackers are reselling stolen access through underground services that Google calls "LLM Mixers."

#5127. One BlackRock fund dominates Bitcoin’s billion-dollar ETF exodus

Fidelity finished positive in the November 2-6 week, but the other funds collectively remained negative without IBIT.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) accounted for 94% of US spot Bitcoin ETFs' net withdrawals in the completed November 2-6 week, leaving one fund responsible for most of the category's retreat. That leaves the next recovery test focused on one fund: can IBIT’s withdrawals slow?

The 12 funds tracked by Farside Investors recorded weekly net outflows of $1,282 million. IBIT recorded net outflows of $1,210 million. Fidelity's Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC) moved in the opposite direction, recording weekly net inflows of $93 million.

IBIT's share was 94.4% of the aggregate net withdrawal, after positive flows elsewhere offset part of the withdrawals. The denominator is net fund flows across the group, not gross redemptions or all Bitcoin selling.

All funds other than IBIT collectively recorded net outflows of $72 million during the week. Removing IBIT's withdrawals from that calculation would substantially reduce the shortfall while leaving the remaining group negative.

The daily pattern also matters. IBIT recorded withdrawals in each of the five sessions, while the group finished positive only on November 4. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of $412 million on November 6.

Fidelity was a counterweight across the week, despite recording withdrawals on Thursday. Three other funds also finished the week positive. The picture was therefore more uneven than a universal exit from Bitcoin funds, although the positive products did not offset the category's largest withdrawal source.

Wednesday's Fidelity-led inflows failed to persist: Thursday's withdrawals restored the negative aggregate reading, and Friday ended the week with another outflow.

iShares reported IBIT net assets of about $61 billion as of November 6. The week's withdrawals were roughly 2% of that ending asset base.

Redemptions also need care when connecting fund flows to Bitcoin selling. The IBIT prospectus describes both cash and in-kind settlement. A cash redemption involves the trust selling bitcoin and delivering cash. An in-kind redemption delivers bitcoin to an authorized participant, the intermediary handling the redemption, or its designated agent or client.

#5126. Bitcoin Price Holds Near $75,000 After Hot October Jobs Report

U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, nearly three times the 59,000 economists expected, the Labor Department said Friday, and the bitcoin price briefly pushed above $76,100 before settling near $75,500, Bitcoin Magazine Pro data shows.

The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from 4.2%, beating the Dow Jones forecast that called for it to hold. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% over the year, both ahead of estimates, CNBC reported.

Prior months were revised higher as well. August payrolls moved to 186,000, an upward revision of 53,000, and September rose to 60,000 after a 31,000 upgrade, leaving the two-month total 84,000 stronger than first reported.

The print lands on a market still digesting Thursday’s Nasdaq-led rout. The bitcoin price had held near $76,000 into that close, dipped toward $75,200 late in the session, then recovered into the mid-$75,000s overnight before the 8:30 a.m. ET release. Spot bitcoin changed hands around $75,800 after the data, with a market cap of about $1.52 trillion and roughly $48 billion in trading volume over the past day, Yahoo Finance data indicated.

Bitcoin price’s first move was a quick spike above $76,100, then a slide toward $75,600 before it settled back near $75,800. The range on the day has run from about $75,240 to $76,280, leaving the market little changed from its pre-release level even as rate futures repriced.

That muted finish fits the pattern after big macro prints. Most of the damage to the bitcoin price this week came from equity risk-off, not from the labor market itself, and a hot payrolls number mainly reinforces the path the Fed was already pricing.

CME FedWatch odds put roughly a 79% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the Dec. 9 meeting after the release, up from about 70% into the open. The next employment report is due Dec. 4, five days before that decision, and the signal points the same way the last Fed hold did: stronger hiring and firmer wages leave less room for another pause.

Thursday’s session still sets the floor under the bitcoin price. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5% and dropped into correction territory, more than 10% below its recent high, while the S&P 500 lost about 4.4% and the Dow shed roughly 1,800 points, or 3.4%, CNBC reported.

The Magnificent Seven erased more than $1 trillion in market value. Nvidia alone lost more than 9%, wiping out roughly $440 billion in capitalization, as investors priced in a slower AI data-center buildout after the Democratic midterm sweep.

Bitcoin has traded with that AI-heavy complex for most of the year, so a correction in the Nasdaq has pulled the bitcoin price lower even when on-chain flows looked steady. Miners that leased power and floor space to AI tenants are caught in both trades.

Fund flows followed the risk-off tape. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs posted $430.2 million in net outflows on Thursday, led by about $200 million from Fidelity’s FBTC and roughly $105 million from BlackRock’s IBIT, bringing week-to-date redemptions through Thursday to about $870 million.

Leverage kept the bitcoin price soft into the overnight. More than $1 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, mostly long bets built during Wednesday’s short-squeeze bounce that lifted bitcoin near $80,000.

Professional and business services led October hiring with 70,000 jobs, health care added 42,000, and transportation and warehousing gained 25,000. Manufacturing rose 19,000. The breadth undercuts the recent pattern in which health care carried most of the gains.

Policy risk has not eased either. House Democrats are already drafting their own market structure bill ahead of taking the committees in January, a backdrop that has hung over crypto equities since the midterm results first hit the bitcoin price.

Traders are watching whether the bitcoin price can defend the mid-$75,000 zone that held on election night and several times since August. A clean break would leave September’s low back in sight after a week that erased most of the post-election squeeze, now with a hotter labor market and firmer hike odds stacked on top.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $75,500.

#5125. The diesel problem that could spoil Bitcoin’s hopes for cheaper money

National inventories fell to 99.26 million barrels, while lower weekly diesel and heating-oil prices kept the financing risk conditional.

U.S. inventories of distillate fuel oil, which includes diesel and heating oil, fell below 100 million barrels in the week ended Oct. 30, even as the latest surveyed fuel prices declined. The smaller stock buffer leaves fuel costs a potential obstacle to inflation relief and easier financing for Bitcoin investors.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's Nov. 4 report showed stocks of 99.26 million barrels, down from 102.82 million a week earlier. That 3.57-million-barrel decline left inventories 13% below their five-year average.

U.S. on-highway diesel averaged $6.29 a gallon on Nov. 2, down 6 cents in a week. EIA's surveyed residential heating-oil average fell 9.2 cents to $6.14 a gallon over the same period. Diesel prices include taxes; the heating-oil series excludes them.

Both fuels remained substantially more expensive than a year earlier: diesel was up $2.54 a gallon and residential heating oil was up $2.51.

There is also continuing refinery supply. Utilization increased to 94.5% from 92.8% in the week ended Oct. 30, although distillate production edged down to 5.154 million barrels a day from 5.161 million. Higher overall refinery activity therefore coexisted with a further draw on distillate stocks.

Diesel powers freight, while heating oil adds directly to household bills. Persistent fuel costs can make moving goods and heating homes more expensive. If that pressure slows broader inflation relief, it could obstruct easier financing conditions for Bitcoin investors.

Historical research explains why that possibility matters. Authors of the August 2023 International Monetary Fund working paper The Crypto Cycle and US Monetary Policy found that Fed tightening reduced a common crypto-price measure through investors' willingness to take risk.

The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28 and said inflation remained elevated. That decision preceded the inventory release.

EIA's next weekly petroleum report is scheduled for Nov. 12 at noon Eastern, covering the week ended Nov. 6. Sustained inventory rebuilding alongside lower fuel costs would weaken the inflation concern. Continued draws would keep attention on the stock buffer, but their significance for Bitcoin would depend on whether fuel pressure reaches broader inflation and financing conditions.

#5123. Binance Cuts Off SignalPlus API Keys Over 'Potential Security Issue' at Trading Platform

Binance Cuts Off SignalPlus API Keys Over 'Potential Security Issue' at Trading Platform

Binance has removed all API keys linked to SignalPlus, a third-party crypto trading platform, after SignalPlus reported a "potential security issue," the exchange said on Thursday.

"Binance's own systems are unaffected. User funds remain safe," the exchange said, describing the move as an "immediate precautionary measure."

Following a potential security issue reported by third-party platform SignalPlus, we have proactively removed all API keys linked to SignalPlus as an immediate precautionary measure.

Binance's own systems are unaffected. User funds remain safe.

If you used SignalPlus, please… pic.twitter.com/0HYYkTAW2p

API keys let third-party apps and trading tools connect to a user's exchange account and place trades on their behalf. Removing them cuts off that connection, meaning any automated strategies running on Binance through SignalPlus will stop until users set up new keys.

Binance urged SignalPlus users to log into their accounts directly to review their positions and open orders. It recommended that they wait until SignalPlus confirms the issue is fully resolved before reconnecting, and that they always enable IP whitelisting, which restricts an API key to approved internet addresses.

The exchange also called on all third-party platforms integrated with Binance to review their security controls, watch for unusual activity and contact it immediately if they spot any concerns.

SignalPlus, a Hong Kong-based platform that provides trading tools for crypto options and derivatives, connects to several exchanges, including Binance.

The incident comes a week after Binance was hit by the largest hack in crypto history, in which attackers drained about $6.4 billion from its hot wallets on October 29. The FBI has attributed the theft to North Korean hackers it calls TraderTraitor, a claim Pyongyang has denied.

Binance has said the attack began when a fake recruiter persuaded one of its engineers to download a malware-laced coding assignment, and that the attackers then used stolen credentials to reach an internal wallet signing service.

Binance said on Wednesday that it has replenished about 98% of the stolen assets from its own funds, and is still buying the rest, mostly less liquid tokens, through market and over-the-counter channels. It has also taken a new proof-of-reserves snapshot covering 44 tokens, up from 10, which users will be able to verify once its zero-knowledge proof is generated in about 50 to 60 hours.

The exchange is still restoring services. On Thursday, it began reopening withdrawals for more assets in phases, prioritizing tokens based on user demand over the past week. Deposits remain open.
